A few colleagues have asked what I use and recommend for working with large language models (LLMs) like Claude and ChatGPT — in research, writing, and teaching. This is a running, informal list rather than institutional guidance; treat it as one colleague's notes.

# AI or Me
I found it useful in my work to create a table of tasks and identify whether or not I want to delegate them to an LLM or do them myself. Your own table may look different.

## Organization of researchtasks

| Task | LLM |
| --- | --- |
| Organization | Delegate |
| Extraction | Delegate |
| Finding passages | Assist |
| Paper searches | Assist |
| Summarize a paper I haven't read | Caution! |
| Evaluate paper's contribution or importance | Me first |
| Identify and define conceptual categories and frameworks | Me first, maybe AI react |
| Development of theoretical framework | Me |
| Summarize a paper I have read | Delegate |

## AI Log
I find it useful to keep a running log of my own AI use in my scholarly work so I can track what I did so that I can retrace my work and share if necessary.

# Getting Started

- [Anthropic's Claude](https://claude.ai) — the assistant I use most for research and writing tasks.
- [OpenAI's ChatGPT](https://chatgpt.com) — the most widely used alternative; useful to know if students are using it.
- [The Bullshit Machines](https://thebullshitmachines.com/index.html) — a free short course on how LLMs work and where they mislead; a good starting point for critical, informed use.
- [Claude Academy course catalog](https://academy.claude.com/courses) — structured video courses on AI fundamentals, using Claude, and AI fluency for various professional roles.

# Using LLMs in Research and Writing

- [My Claude skills](https://github.com/jasosmith/skills) — a collection of skills I use in my own research and writing workflows.
- [Lawve](https://lawve.ai/) — a hub for legal professionals to discover, download, and share AI agent skills for Claude, ChatGPT, and Gemini.
- [Beaver](https://www.beaverapp.ai/) — an AI research assistant integrated into Zotero, with sentence-level citations for searching your library and reading papers.
- [Andrej Karpathy: append-and-review knowledge bases](https://gist.github.com/karpathy/442a6bf555914893e9891c11519de94f) — a pattern for having an LLM incrementally read sources and maintain a compounding wiki, instead of re-retrieving raw documents each time. I am using this approach in building a wiki for course management and prep.

# Using LLMs in Teaching

- [LegalEd.AI](https://legaled.ai/) — explorations in using AI to teach and learn the law, with news, articles, and tool guidance for law students and educators.
- [AI Fluency for Educators](https://academy.claude.com/courses/ai-fluency-for-educators) (Claude Academy) — a course on applying the "4D" AI Fluency Framework (Delegation, Description, Discernment, Diligence) to teaching practice and course design.

# Further Reading

- [CSU Generative AI](https://genai.calstate.edu/) — the CSU system's generative AI initiative and resource hub; useful for CSU-specific guidance.
- [One Useful Thing](https://www.oneusefulthing.org/) — Ethan Mollick's newsletter on the implications of AI for work, education, and life.
- [AAC&U: AI](https://www.aacu.org/trending-topics/ai) — resources, events, and initiatives from the Association of American Colleges & Universities on integrating AI into teaching, learning, and institutional practice.
- [MIT Education and AI Report, January 2026](https://aiandeducation.mit.edu/) 
- *Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans*, Melaine Mitchell (2023).
- *The Alignment Problem*, Brian Christian (2020).
